newsitem.title: UK: NATO military structure should be slashed - Ruehe.
newsitem.headline: NATO military structure should be slashed - Ruehe.

text.p: NATO's military structure will have to be slashed as part of wide-ranging reforms to help the alliance adapt to the post-Cold War world, German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Tuesday.

Military chiefs of staff from NATO are expected to propose a new, leaner command structure when they meet in Brussels later this week to make recommendations to the alliance's political leaders on how NATO should work in the future.

"The new military structure will reflect the emphasis on crisis management and cooperation. It will reflect a new balance of burden and responsibility sharing between Europe and North America," Ruehe said.
"And it will be determined by drastic horizontal and vertical rationalisation. We'll probably go down from 60 headquarters to 30," he told the Royal Institute of International Affairs in London.

Discussion on NATO restructuring has centred on whether to cut back on the number of regional commands, which now number three in the Atlantic and three in Europe. There are also several dozen local command headquarters.
NATO heads of government are due to hold a summit next year when they will discuss the reforms as well as inviting some countries in eastern Europe to open negotiations on membership.

The reform process involves the creation of a distinct European security identity within the alliance as well as boosting links with the smaller and less powerful Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping.
Ruehe said NATO and WEU could avoid wasting resources by using the same structures and said all members had to realise that the alliance was entering a new era.
"Not everything can stay as it is. Nobody is entitled to claim disproportionate influence in the new political and strategic environment," he said.

Ruehe said NATO should concentrate on relations with Russia, which is angry over the alliance's plans for expansion, and try to reassure those countries in eastern Europe who would have to wait before being allowed to join.

"The political and conceptual link between enlargement of NATO and that of the European Union is important and must be exploited," he said. "We should at all costs avoid creating the shock of a double rejection."
NATO has not named the countries most likely to be given membership but it is an open secret that Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovenia are the front-runners.
